did_you_know.text: Did you know? David declares at the very beginning of the psalm: “In the LORD I have taken refuge”—the LORD is his source of shelter, and therefore he rejects the advice to flee to the mountain like a bird escaping.

Did you know? The expression “Flee... to your mountain like a bird” presents the advice to escape in vivid language: the speaker is urged to leave his place and fly to the mountain, but this advice conflicts with his trust in the LORD.
Did you know? The wicked are portrayed as already drawing the bow and preparing the arrow to shoot “in the darkness”—secretly and under cover of night—at those who are upright in heart.

Did you know? The word “foundations” refers to basic supports or structures, and the verse asks what the righteous can do when the foundations are destroyed. In this way, it emphasizes the severity of the moral and social crisis.
Did you know? The psalm places the LORD in two exalted locations: in His holy temple and in heaven, and immediately emphasizes that His eyes and eyelids examine humanity.
Did you know? According to the verse, the LORD does not merely observe people but also tests the righteous; at the same time, He rejects the wicked and those who love violence.

Did you know? The punishment of the wicked is described through vivid images of snares, fire, sulfur, and scorching wind; all of these are presented as “the portion of their cup,” meaning the share appointed to them.

Did you know? The psalm concludes by presenting the LORD as One who loves righteousness and placing the upright before Him: “The upright will behold His face.” Thus, the psalm ends by contrasting the fate of the wicked with the upright’s nearness to the LORD.
